items.explanation: Monroe argued that east of the Mississippi, Native peoples would face endless harassment from settlers, so removal west — however coercive in practice — was presented as being in their interest.
options: A. They would escape constant harassment west of the Mississippi
B. The army would protect them on the journey west
C. They would be fairly paid for the lands they left
D. Western settlers welcomed Native neighbors
items.stem: President Monroe claimed westward removal would benefit Native Americans because

option_explanations.A: Correct. Monroe argued that east of the Mississippi, Native peoples would face constant harassment from settlers, so moving west — however coercive in practice — was presented as being in their own interest.
option_explanations.B: The army did not protect Native peoples on the journey west. Removal was enforced by soldiers and proved deadly — the Trail of Tears killed thousands — not a guarded, safe migration.
option_explanations.C: Native peoples were not fairly paid for the lands they left. Treaties were signed under duress and compensation was a fraction of the land's value — unfair payment was not Monroe's stated benefit.
option_explanations.D: Western settlers did not welcome Native neighbors. Settler pressure for Native land was the very reason removal was proposed, so 'welcoming neighbors' reverses the history.

items.explanation: South Carolina, enraged by the protective tariffs of 1828 and 1832, declared them null within the state — the Nullification Crisis that Jackson answered with the Force Bill.
options: A. Georgia defied Congress over slavery
B. South Carolina nullified Indian-removal laws
C. South Carolina nullified the federal tariff bills
D. Southern electors bolted in the 1824 election
items.stem: Nullification became a national issue when

option_explanations.A: Georgia did defy federal authority, but over Cherokee removal — ignoring the Supreme Court in Worcester v. Georgia — not over slavery, and that was not what made nullification a national crisis.
option_explanations.B: South Carolina did not nullify Indian-removal laws. Indian removal was a federal policy the South generally supported; the nullified laws were the protective tariffs.
option_explanations.C: Correct. South Carolina, enraged by the protective tariffs of 1828 and 1832, declared them null and void within the state — the Nullification Crisis that Jackson answered with the Force Bill.
option_explanations.D: Southern electors did not bolt in the 1824 election over nullification. The 'corrupt bargain' election of 1824 was a different controversy, about the House choosing Adams over Jackson.

items.explanation: Jackson's enemies called him a backwoods tyrant who empowered the presidency and ruled through his informal 'Kitchen Cabinet' — but no one could say he lacked experience: he had been a congressman, senator, judge, and general.
options: A. He was a common man unfit for the presidency
B. He aggrandized presidential power
C. He lacked experience in public affairs
D. He governed through his 'Kitchen Cabinet'
items.stem: Critics of Andrew Jackson made all of the following charges EXCEPT that

option_explanations.A: This was a real charge: Adams's supporters painted Jackson as an unfit backwoodsman — a 'military chieftain' unqualified for the presidency.
option_explanations.B: This was a real charge: opponents called him 'King Andrew' for aggrandizing presidential power, especially in the Bank War and the removal of deposits.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. No one could charge Jackson with lacking public experience: he had been a congressman, a senator, a territorial judge, and a victorious general.
option_explanations.D: This was a real charge: critics attacked Jackson for governing through his informal 'Kitchen Cabinet' of advisers rather than his official cabinet.

items.explanation: The mills hired young farm women ('mill girls'), ran on water power, and saw little unrest before the 1830s–40s — but they used the factory system, which replaced the older putting-out system of home production.
options: A. Women made up much of their workforce
B. They depended on water power
C. They organized work through the putting-out system
D. Labor unrest was rare before the 1830s
items.stem: All of the following are true of early New England textile mills EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: This is true of the early mills: young farm women — the 'mill girls' of Lowell — made up much of the workforce.
option_explanations.B: This is true: the early mills depended on water power from rivers like the Merrimack to run their machinery.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. The mills did not use the putting-out system; they used the factory system, which replaced the older putting-out arrangement of home-based production.
option_explanations.D: This is true: labor unrest was rare before the 1830s–40s, when wage cuts and longer hours finally sparked strikes and the Lowell women's protests.

items.explanation: As Massachusetts secretary of education, Mann crusaded for free public schools, better teacher training, and longer school terms — the father of the common-school movement.
options: A. Abolitionism
B. Temperance
C. Prison reform
D. Public-school reform

option_explanations.A: Mann was not an abolitionist leader; that cause belonged to figures like William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass.
option_explanations.B: Mann was not a temperance crusader; the temperance movement's leaders included Neal Dow and the Washingtonians.
option_explanations.C: Mann was not a prison reformer; Dorothea Dix led the campaign for asylums and better treatment of the mentally ill.
option_explanations.D: Correct. As Massachusetts secretary of education, Horace Mann crusaded for free public schools, better teacher training, and longer school terms — the father of the common-school movement.

items.explanation: Jackson saw the Bank as a privileged monopoly — 'the rich and powerful' bending government to their will — and vetoed its recharter as undemocratic.
options: A. It was an undemocratic financial monopoly
B. It meddled in the slavery debate
C. It gave the president too much financial power
D. It refused to fund internal improvements
items.stem: Jackson attacked the Second Bank of the United States because he believed
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

option_explanations.A: Correct. Jackson saw the Bank as a privileged, undemocratic monopoly — 'the rich and powerful' bending government to their will — and vetoed its recharter on those grounds.
option_explanations.B: The Bank did not meddle in the slavery debate. Jackson's quarrel with it was about financial monopoly and democratic control of the currency, not slavery.
option_explanations.C: Jackson's fear ran the other way: he believed the Bank gave too much power to private bankers and foreign stockholders, not to the president.
option_explanations.D: The Bank's refusal to fund internal improvements was not Jackson's complaint. His veto message attacked the Bank as an unconstitutional monopoly, not as a stingy lender.

items.explanation: The Bank's notes and credit underpinned commerce, so northern merchants and manufacturers — who depended on stable banking — opposed its destruction, while planters, western farmers, and laborers cheered Jackson.
options: A. A southern planter
B. A western farmer
C. An urban laborer
D. A northern businessman
items.stem: Who would have been most likely to oppose Jackson's war on the Bank?
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

option_explanations.A: A southern planter would have cheered Jackson's war on the Bank: planters resented the Bank's tight credit and blamed it for their debts.
option_explanations.B: A western farmer would have cheered Jackson: westerners hated the Bank as an eastern money power that foreclosed on farms and restricted credit.
option_explanations.C: An urban laborer would have cheered Jackson: workingmen's groups like the Locofocos opposed all monopolies as enemies of the common man.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Bank's notes and credit underpinned commerce, so northern businessmen — merchants and manufacturers who depended on stable banking — opposed its destruction.

items.explanation: Both presidents used federal power to smash concentrated economic power they deemed corrupt — Jackson killing the Bank, Roosevelt prosecuting the trusts under the Sherman Act.
options: A. Clay's 'American System'
B. McKinley's 'Full Dinner Pail'
C. Theodore Roosevelt's 'trust-busting'
D. Johnson's 'Great Society'
items.stem: Jackson's 'Bank War' is most comparable as a policy to
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

option_explanations.A: Clay's American System is the opposite comparison: it called for a national bank as one of its pillars, while Jackson's Bank War destroyed the Bank.
option_explanations.B: McKinley's 'Full Dinner Pail' was an 1890s–1900 campaign promise of prosperity under the protective tariff — a slogan about abundance, not a campaign against concentrated economic power.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Both presidents used federal power to smash concentrated economic power they deemed corrupt — Jackson killing the Bank, Theodore Roosevelt prosecuting the trusts under the Sherman Act.
option_explanations.D: Johnson's Great Society was a program of anti-poverty and civil-rights legislation in the 1960s — a different domain entirely from Jackson's war on a financial institution.
